note: Each corrects a statement in a new verdict's text that the case's prompt or policyengine-us 2.41.0 contradicts. Two independent reviewers (Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, neither part of the release) read all 26 new texts against each case's prompt and the engine (docs/release_20261013b/design.md); each correction here was then checked against the engine's code and parameters, and for scenario_015's Medicaid pathway against a calculation of that household. None changes a class, a flag, an exclusion or a score.

amendments.old: PolicyEngine's aged/blind/disabled pathway applies SSI-style income limits plus a small resource cap.
amendments.new: PolicyEngine's aged/blind/disabled pathway in Indiana requires SSI's definition of disability, countable income within 100% of the poverty guideline and resources under $2,000.
amendments.reason: The text stated Indiana's rule as a general fact and called the income limit SSI-style. Indiana's parameters under gov.hhs.medicaid.eligibility.categories.senior_or_disabled: income limit 1.00 of the poverty guideline (income/limit/individual.yaml), not the SSI federal benefit rate (uses_ssi_federal_benefit_rate.yaml: false), and a $2,000 individual asset limit (assets/limit/individual.yaml), tested as assets below the limit. The pathway's first condition is is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled (is_optional_senior_or_disabled_for_medicaid).

amendments.old: Roughly $45,000 of earnings and about $585,000 in bank and stock assets fail both tests, so medicaid_category is NONE.
amendments.new: Earnings of $45,000 are above SSI's substantial gainful activity limit, so PolicyEngine does not count the head as disabled for this pathway, and about $585,000 in bank and stock assets is far above the resource cap, so medicaid_category is NONE.
amendments.reason: The engine's income test does not fail here; the disability condition and the asset test do. Computed for this household on policyengine-us 2.41.0: meets_ssi_disability_criteria False, ssi_engaged_in_sga True, is_ssi_disabled False, is_optional_senior_or_disabled_income_eligible True (medicaid_optional_senior_or_disabled_countable_income 0), is_optional_senior_or_disabled_asset_eligible False (ssi_countable_resources 584,850), medicaid_category NONE. ssi_engaged_in_sga compares monthly ssi_earned_income ($3,750) with gov.ssa.sga.non_blind ($1,690 in 2026), and is_ssi_disabled is meets_ssi_disability_criteria and not ssi_engaged_in_sga.

amendments.old: Both models treated the disability flag by itself as qualifying
amendments.new: One model treated the disability flag by itself as qualifying and the other wrongly asserted that the head's income and assets were within the disability limits
amendments.reason: Only minimax-m3 relied on the flag alone. claude-sonnet-5's reasoning in the case's prompt says the head's income is 'well below the SSI/disability-related Medicaid threshold' and that earnings 'plus assets fall within eligibility limits'.

amendments.old: PolicyEngine does not model a working-disabled buy-in with relaxed limits
amendments.new: PolicyEngine models a working-disabled buy-in only for California, Illinois and Mississippi, not Indiana
amendments.reason: True for this household's state but false as a general fact: policyengine-us 2.41.0's is_working_disabled_buy_in_for_medicaid is ca_wdp_eligible or il_hbwd_eligible or ms_wd_eligible, each defined for its own state, and nothing models one for Indiana.

amendments.old: The disability pathway needs SSI-level income and resources
amendments.new: In Indiana the disability pathway needs countable income within 100% of the poverty guideline and resources under $2,000
amendments.reason: Indiana's income limit for the pathway is the poverty guideline, not the SSI benefit rate. Indiana's parameters under gov.hhs.medicaid.eligibility.categories.senior_or_disabled: income limit 1.00 of the poverty guideline (income/limit/individual.yaml), not the SSI federal benefit rate (uses_ssi_federal_benefit_rate.yaml: false), and a $2,000 individual asset limit (assets/limit/individual.yaml), tested as assets below the limit.

amendments.old: It also never compared the full $3,022.97 monthly gross income with the 130% gross limit, which the household fails at about 232% of the guideline.
amendments.new: The full $3,022.97 of monthly gross income fails the 130% gross limit, at about 232% of the guideline.
amendments.reason: The model's reasoning in the case's prompt gives an income limit of about $1,655 a month and says 'This household exceeds the income limit', as the annotation's next sentence also reports, so 'never compared' contradicts both.

amendments.old: The model ran the one-child EITC phase-out on a made-up $27,700 AGI.
amendments.new: The model computed the one-child EITC as $4,450 minus 7.65% of ($72,600 − $27,700), but 7.65% is the childless phase-out rate and the one-child rate is 15.98%.
amendments.reason: The model's reasoning in the case's prompt is '2026 max $4,450 minus 7.65% phaseout × ($72,600 - $27,700 AGI) = $1,015': $72,600 is the income and $27,700 the phase-out start, so the phase-out was not run on a $27,700 AGI. policyengine-us 2.41.0's 2026 EITC phase-out rates are 0.0765 with no children and 0.1598 with one (gov.irs.credits.eitc.phase_out.rate).

amendments.old: Most models treated the $1,700 refundability cap as the amount payable and skipped the step
amendments.new: The most common error treated the $1,700 refundability cap as the amount payable and skipped the step
amendments.reason: Six of the eleven models submitted $1,700 and four of them skipped the limit (claude-opus-4.7, claude-opus-4.8, gpt-5.6-luna, ox-alpha); claude-sonnet-5 applied it and then overrode it, and qwen3.8-max applied it to the child's liability. That is the most common error, not most models.

amendments.old: the Recovery Rebate and payroll tax credits are inactive in 2026
amendments.new: the Recovery Rebate and payroll tax credits are $0 in 2026
amendments.reason: The case's prompt says each component returned $0. In policyengine-us 2.41.0 the refundable payroll tax credit is an input with no dated rule (refundable_payroll_tax_credit has no formula), so 'inactive in 2026' fits only the Recovery Rebate.

amendments.old: Any positive figure means the model either invented a child-based credit or applied the with-children EITC schedule.
amendments.new: Any positive figure is incorrect for this household.
amendments.reason: The case's prompt shows every refundable credit component at $0, which supports rejecting any positive answer but not a claim that these two errors are the only way to reach one. policyengine-us 2.41.0's 2026 EITC at $45,000 of earnings for a single filer is $0 with no child (maximum $664), $1,054 with one and $2,870 with two (gov.irs.credits.eitc max, phase_out.start, phase_out.rate), so $1,735.80 fits none of the 2026 schedules.

amendments.old: The EITC figure only fits the with-children phase-out schedule.
amendments.new: The EITC figure does not fit the childless schedule.
amendments.reason: The model's reasoning in the case's prompt gives $1,735.80 without a schedule. policyengine-us 2.41.0's 2026 EITC at $45,000 of earnings for a single filer is $0 with no child (maximum $664), $1,054 with one and $2,870 with two (gov.irs.credits.eitc max, phase_out.start, phase_out.rate), so $1,735.80 fits none of the 2026 schedules. It exceeds the childless maximum, which is all the record shows.
